clinician.trajectory_summary: A 17-year-old girl presented with 3 weeks of right-sided headache (described as heaviness above the right eye) and horizontal binocular diplopia. Initial outpatient workup included diagnosis of migraine (treated with amitriptyline without improvement) and subsequent ophthalmology evaluation revealing right cranial nerve VI palsy with impaired abduction and esotropia. Initial MRI brain with/without gadolinium was read as normal, and a 7-day prednisone taper was unsuccessful. Upon admission, physical examination confirmed isolated right abducens nerve palsy with esotropia but was otherwise unremarkable (afebrile, intact vision, normal pupillary responses). Eleven days after the initial study, repeat MRI brain and orbits revealed a possible cavernous sinus lesion. Extensive workup ruled out neoplastic and alternative inflammatory causes: CSF studies demonstrated normal cell count, no malignant cells, normal AFP (ruling out germ cell tumor), normal ACE (ruling out sarcoidosis), and negative cultures/PCR panels; serum protein electrophoresis was normal (ruling out lymphoma); and autoimmune/infectious serologies were negative. After multidisciplinary consultation, intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3 days) was administered, resulting in improvement of headaches, diplopia, and slight improvement in right eye abduction. The patient was discharged on a prolonged steroid taper with ophthalmology follow-up. The diagnosis of Tolosa-Hunt syndrome was established based on the presentation of painful ophthalmoplegia, radiographic evidence of a cavernous sinus lesion, exclusion of neoplastic processes (negative CSF cytology and SPEP), and characteristic dramatic response to high-dose corticosteroids.
